grid.text: Efficacy and safety of ThrombEctomy iN Stroke with extended leSION and extended time window: a randomized, controlled trial

This study is an investigator-initiated, prospective, open label, blinded endpoint (PROBE), multinational, European, two-arm, randomized, controlled, post-market study to compare the safety and effectiveness of endovascular thrombectomy as compared to best medical care alone in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) in patients with extended stroke lesions defined by an ASPECT score of 3-5 and in an extended time window (up to 12 hours from symptom onset or last seen well). This is an adaptive design study with interim analyses with pre-specified stopping rules allowing for the possibility of early termination based on either a determination of study success or futility.

Up to 665 subjects will be enrolled in the study and randomized for the Intention to Treat analysis set. The randomization will be stratified by time from symptom onset or last seen well (< 6h and 6-11h), stroke severity (NIHSS ≤18, NIHSS >18) Interim data analysis is planned after the primary endpoint has been obtained for one third and two thirds of the patients. At each of these sample sizes, the available 90-day mRS data for each treatment arm will be evaluated. Safety interim analysis will be performed after one third and two thirds of the patients have been included.
Subjects who meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to one of the following two treatment arms: Arm 1: best medical care Arm 2: endovascular thrombectomy and best medical care

The study assessments include: • Screening/Baseline • Study Treatment (per randomization) • Follow up visit at 24 (-/+ 6) hours post hospitalization • Hospital Discharge visit (or 7 (+3) days, whichever comes first) • Post Treatment Follow-up Visit at Day 90 (+/- 14 days) (alternatively standardized telephone interview) • Post Treatment Follow-Up interview / self-administered questionnaire at 12 month (+/- 14 days)

Interim Analysis and Early Stopping Rules

Interim data analysis is planned starting after one third and two thirds of the patients have been randomized and evaluated for the 90-day mRS endpoint. If interim analysis data are sufficient to demonstrate study success, then the trial enrollment will be terminated early. If interim analysis data indicate that study success is highly unlikely even if enrollment were to continue to a maximum sample size of 665, then the trial enrollment will be terminated early for futility. The decision to stop or continue the trial will be based on the overall assessment of risk and benefit by the steering committee, supported by the DSMB. Safety interim analysis will be performed after one third and two thirds of the patients have been included.

grid.text: Efficacy and safety of ThrombEctomy iN Stroke with extended leSION and extended time window: a randomized, controlled trial

This study is an investigator-initiated, prospective, open label, blinded endpoint (PROBE), multinational, European, two-arm, randomized, controlled, post-market study to compare the safety and effectiveness of endovascular thrombectomy as compared to best medical care alone in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) in patients with extended stroke lesions defined by an ASPECT score of 3-5 and in an extended time window (up to 12 hours from symptom onset or last seen well). This is an adaptive design study with interim analyses with pre-specified stopping rules allowing for the possibility of early termination based on either a determination of study success or futility.

Up to 665 subjects will be enrolled in the study and randomized for the Intention to Treat analysis set. The randomization will be stratified by time from symptom onset or last seen well (< 6h and 6-11h), stroke severity (NIHSS ≤18, NIHSS >18) Interim data analysis is planned after the primary endpoint has been obtained for one third and two thirds of the patients. At each of these sample sizes, the available 90-day mRS data for each treatment arm will be evaluated. Safety interim analysis will be performed after one third and two thirds of the patients have been included.
Subjects who meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized in a 1:1 ratio to one of the following two treatment arms: Arm 1: best medical care Arm 2: endovascular thrombectomy and best medical care

The primary objective of this study is to test efficacy and safety of thrombectomy in acute stroke patients with uncertain benefit of endovascular stroke treatment, i.e. extended ischemic lesion size with an ASPECT score of 3-5 up to 12 hours from symptom onset or last seen well as compared to best medical care alone.

Patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke (AIS) based on focal occlusion in the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), and/or the intracranial segment of the distal internal carotid artery (ICA), determined by MRA or CTA, and who meet all eligibility criteria will be considered for study enrollment.
Clinical inclusion criteria: • Moderate to severe stroke (NIHSS <26) • Premorbid modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-2

grid.text: • Life expectancy > 12 months • Age >18 years • Treatment can be accomplished within 12 hours after stroke onset (if known) or last seen well, i.e. randomization within 11 hours after ictus or last seen well • Informed consent by the patient, legal guardian, or inclusion of patient under presumptive will after consultation of an independent physician and statement of investigator according to local approval Imaging inclusion criteria • Occlusion of the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), and/or the intracranial segment of the distal internal carotid artery (ICA), determined by MRA or CTA • CT (non-contrast-CT) or DWI with an ASPECT score of 3-5

Clinical exclusion criteria • active participant in another drug or device treatment trial unless approved by Sponsor. • Patient has pre-existing neurological or psychiatric disease that could impede the study results or would confound the neurological or functional evaluations. • Patient has history of contraindication for contrast medium. • Patient is known to have infective endocarditis • Patient's anticipated life expectancy is less than 12 months Imaging exclusion criteria • Extracranial CT or MR angiography showing high grade stenosis expected to require acute stent placement (e.g. ICA stenting) during the procedure • CT or MRI with evidence of mass effect or intracranial tumor • If CT perfusion is done per institutional standard: CBV drop on CTP with an ASPECT score of 0-2

The study assessments include: • Screening/Baseline • Study Treatment (per randomization) • Follow up visit at 24 (-/+ 6) hours post hospitalization • Hospital Discharge visit (or 7 (+3) days, whichever comes first) • Post Treatment Follow-up Visit at Day 90 (+/- 14 days) (alternatively standardized telephone interview) • Post Treatment Follow-Up interview / self-administered questionnaire at 12 month (+/- 14 days)

The primary endpoint of the trial is the mRS outcome at 90 (±14) days post-stroke. The primary effectiveness endpoint analysis is a chi-square test of the difference in linear trends in ordinal mRS outcomes at 90 (±14) days post-stroke between treatment groups ('mRS shift analysis').

The following secondary effectiveness endpoints will be compared between the two treatment groups: • Independent neurological outcome (mRS≤2) at 90 (±14) days • Moderate neurological outcome (mRS≤3) with 90 (±14) days • Rates of decompressive craniotomy • Infarct volume at 24 (±6) hours (CT or MRI) post randomization.

Interim Analysis and Early Stopping Rules

Interim data analysis is planned starting after one third and two thirds of the patients have been randomized and evaluated for the 90-day mRS endpoint. If interim analysis data are sufficient to demonstrate study success, then the trial enrollment will be terminated early. If interim analysis data indicate that study success is highly unlikely even if enrollment were to continue to a maximum sample size of 665, then the trial enrollment will be terminated early for futility. The decision to stop or continue the trial will be based on the overall assessment of risk and benefit by the steering committee, supported by the DSMB. Safety interim analysis will be performed after one third and two thirds of the patients have been included.

In the EU stroke accounts for just over 500.000 deaths each year with just around one in ten men (9%) and one in eight women (12%) dying from stroke (Allender et al., 2008).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The prognosis following an acute ischemic stroke varies, depending on the stroke severity and the individual's premorbid condition, age, and post stroke complications (Adams 1999). In the United  States,  20%  of  individuals  die  within  the  first  year  after  a  first-time  stroke.    The Framingham  Heart  Study  showed  that  among  stroke  survivors,  31%  needed  help  caring  for themselves, 20% needed help when walking, and 71% had impaired vocational capacity when examined an average 7 years following the stroke.
texts.text: The prognosis following an acute ischemic stroke varies, depending on the stroke severity and the individual's premorbid condition, age, and post stroke complications (Adams 1999). In the United  States,  20%  of  individuals  die  within  the  first  year  after  a  first-time  stroke.    The Framingham  Heart  Study  showed  that  among  stroke  survivors,  31%  needed  help  caring  for themselves, 20% needed help when walking, and 71% had impaired vocational capacity when examined an average 7 years following the stroke.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For  years,  intravenous  thrombolysis  with  recombinant  tissue  Plasminogen  Activator  (rtPA, Alteplase)  represented  the  only  effective  and  approved  specific  treatment  for  acute  ischemic stroke  and  is  recommended by international,  European and national guidelines (ESO, 2008). Following  the  first  positive  clinical  trial  of  thrombolysis  in  ischemic  stroke,  treatment  with Alteplase  was  restricted  to  treatment  initiation  ≤3  hours  of  symptom  onset  but  based  on  the results of ECASS III (Hacke et al., 2008) international guidelines now recommend intravenous thrombolysis  up  to  4.5  hours  of  symptom  onset  (Del  Zoppo  et  al.,  2009).  Consequently,  the European Medicines Agency has approved intravenous thrombolysis with Alteplase for acute stroke up to 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
texts.text: For  years,  intravenous  thrombolysis  with  recombinant  tissue  Plasminogen  Activator  (rtPA, Alteplase)  represented  the  only  effective  and  approved  specific  treatment  for  acute  ischemic stroke  and  is  recommended by international,  European and national guidelines (ESO, 2008). Following  the  first  positive  clinical  trial  of  thrombolysis  in  ischemic  stroke,  treatment  with Alteplase  was  restricted  to  treatment  initiation  ≤3  hours  of  symptom  onset  but  based  on  the results of ECASS III (Hacke et al., 2008) international guidelines now recommend intravenous thrombolysis  up  to  4.5  hours  of  symptom  onset  (Del  Zoppo  et  al.,  2009).  Consequently,  the European Medicines Agency has approved intravenous thrombolysis with Alteplase for acute stroke up to 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In large vessel occlusions, however, recanalization after i.v. thrombolysis is infrequent and in a thrombus  length  of  more  than  8  mm  almost  absent  (Riedel  et  al.,  2011).  Since  timely recanalization is crucial for a good outcome in stroke alternative therapy is warranted in patients with large vessel occlusion. Moreover, a substantial number of patients cannot receive i.v. tPA for contraindications (e.g. anticoagulation, recent surgery, time after symptom onset beyond 4.5 hours). In these patient groups endovascular mechanical clot removal has been advocated. The first  generation  devices  (Merci,  Penumbra)  achieved  recanalization  in  up  to  50%;  however, clinical  outcome  was  not  substantially  improved  compared  to  historical  controls  (Smith  et  al., Stroke 2005). Safety of endovascular treatment with mechanical or pharmacological approaches  was  also  comparable  in  patients  under  oral  anticoagulants  (de  Marchis  et  al., 2011). Stent-like devices for thrombectomy also referred to as stent-retrievers have substantially improved recanalization rates and outcome compared to first generation devices (Nogueira et al., 2012, Saver et al., 2012). Recently, 5 RCTs mostly using thrombectomy by stent retrievers in  the  endovascular  treatment  of  acute  stroke  compared  to  best  medical  care  demonstrated overwhelming clinical benefit without increased adverse events (Berkhemer et al., 2015, Goyal et al., 2015, Saver et al., 2015, Campbell et al., 2015, Jovin et al, 2015). However, in these trials mostly patients with good prognostic factors (i.e. short time interval between stroke onset and endovascular  treatment  as  well  as  small  size  of  ischemic  lesion  prior  to  treatment)  were included. Of 1.287 patients randomized, less than 5% were treated >6 hours of symptom onset. With regards to early ischemic signs, in four of these five trials patients with ASPECTS <6 or <7 were excluded. Only MR CLEAN did not specify pre-treatment ASPECTS values as exclusion criterion,  but  even  in  MR  CLEAN  only  small  numbers  of  patients  with  low  ASPECTS  values were included. In 28 patients with ASPECTS 0-4 no treatment effect was evident with an OR of 1.1 (95% CI 0.1-8.4) for benefit in the thrombectomy group, while in 92 patients with ASPECTS 5-7 with an OR of 2.0 (0.9-4.4) a clear trend for a treatment benefit was observed similar to the effect in the group of patients with ASPECTS >7 (Berkhemer et al., 2015). Thus, based on the data from these trials, insufficient evidence is available to judge whether mechanical thrombectomy is also safe and effective in patients with an extended time window or advanced signs of early ischemia, or a combination of both. This was also acknowledged by experts from the  European  Stroke  Organisation  (ESO),  the  European  Society  for  Minimally  Invasive Neurological  Therapy  (ESMINT),  and  the  European  Society  of  Neuroradiology  (ESNR)  a consensus statement on thrombectomy (Wahlgren et al, 2016). In this statement the experts clearly recommend further randomized clinical trials addressing open issues such as 'treatment in  a  late  und  unknown  time  windows,  treating  patients  with  imaging  findings  not  sufficiently covered  in  recent  trials…'.  TENSION  aims  to  close  this  gap  and  provide  evidence  for thrombectomy in in both late time window and patients with more extend early ischemic signs before treatment.
texts.text: In large vessel occlusions, however, recanalization after i.v. thrombolysis is infrequent and in a thrombus  length  of  more  than  8  mm  almost  absent  (Riedel  et  al.,  2011).  Since  timely recanalization is crucial for a good outcome in stroke alternative therapy is warranted in patients with large vessel occlusion. Moreover, a substantial number of patients cannot receive i.v. tPA for contraindications (e.g. anticoagulation, recent surgery, time after symptom onset beyond 4.5 hours). In these patient groups endovascular mechanical clot removal has been advocated. The first  generation  devices  (Merci,  Penumbra)  achieved  recanalization  in  up  to  50%;  however, clinical  outcome  was  not  substantially  improved  compared  to  historical  controls  (Smith  et  al., Stroke 2005). Safety of endovascular treatment with mechanical or pharmacological approaches  was  also  comparable  in  patients  under  oral  anticoagulants  (de  Marchis  et  al., 2011). Stent-like devices for thrombectomy also referred to as stent-retrievers have substantially improved recanalization rates and outcome compared to first generation devices (Nogueira et al., 2012, Saver et al., 2012). Recently, 5 RCTs mostly using thrombectomy by stent retrievers in  the  endovascular  treatment  of  acute  stroke  compared  to  best  medical  care  demonstrated overwhelming clinical benefit without increased adverse events (Berkhemer et al., 2015, Goyal et al., 2015, Saver et al., 2015, Campbell et al., 2015, Jovin et al, 2015). However, in these trials mostly patients with good prognostic factors (i.e. short time interval between stroke onset and endovascular  treatment  as  well  as  small  size  of  ischemic  lesion  prior  to  treatment)  were included. Of 1.287 patients randomized, less than 5% were treated >6 hours of symptom onset. With regards to early ischemic signs, in four of these five trials patients with ASPECTS <6 or <7 were excluded. Only MR CLEAN did not specify pre-treatment ASPECTS values as exclusion criterion,  but  even  in  MR  CLEAN  only  small  numbers  of  patients  with  low  ASPECTS  values were included. In 28 patients with ASPECTS 0-4 no treatment effect was evident with an OR of 1.1 (95% CI 0.1-8.4) for benefit in the thrombectomy group, while in 92 patients with ASPECTS 5-7 with an OR of 2.0 (0.9-4.4) a clear trend for a treatment benefit was observed similar to the effect in the group of patients with ASPECTS >7 (Berkhemer et al., 2015). Thus, based on the data from these trials, insufficient evidence is available to judge whether mechanical thrombectomy is also safe and effective in patients with an extended time window or advanced signs of early ischemia, or a combination of both. This was also acknowledged by experts from the  European  Stroke  Organisation  (ESO),  the  European  Society  for  Minimally  Invasive Neurological  Therapy  (ESMINT),  and  the  European  Society  of  Neuroradiology  (ESNR)  a consensus statement on thrombectomy (Wahlgren et al, 2016). In this statement the experts clearly recommend further randomized clinical trials addressing open issues such as 'treatment in  a  late  und  unknown  time  windows,  treating  patients  with  imaging  findings  not  sufficiently covered  in  recent  trials…'.  TENSION  aims  to  close  this  gap  and  provide  evidence  for thrombectomy in in both late time window and patients with more extend early ischemic signs before treatment.

texts.orig: This is an investigator-initiated, prospective, European, two-arm, randomized, controlled, open label, blinded endpoint post-market study to compare  the  safety and  effectiveness of endovascular thrombectomy compared to best medical treatment alone in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients with extended stroke lesions up to 12 hours of symptom onset or last seen well. Patients who meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized to one of the following two treatment arms: best medical care alone or best medical care plus endovascular treatment with devices for  endovascular  thrombectomy  (referred  to  as  thrombectomy).  Endpoints  in  this  prospective open label study will be assessed blinded to the treatment assignment of the patient (PROBE design).  This  study  will  be  conducted  in  approximately  40  sites  in  eight  to  ten  European countries.    This  is  an  adaptive  design  study,  in  which  there  are  prospectively  stated  interim analyses with specified stopping rules, which allow for the possibility of the study to terminate early  based  on  either  a  determination  of  study  success  or  of  the  futility  to  continue  further enrollment.

texts.orig: If  the  subject  is  randomized  to  the  thrombectomy  arm,  then  the  steps  for  the  endovascular procedure  should  be  subsequently  completed;  groin  puncture  should  be  no  later  than  90 minutes from inclusion imaging.  If a subject randomized to thrombectomy fails the angiographic screening, endovascular procedure should proceed as clinically recommended, and subject will remain in ITT population. If a subject randomized to thrombectomy arm shows rapidly improving neurologic  symptoms  prior  to  procedure,  endovascular  procedure  should  not  proceed,  but subject will remain in ITT population.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All subjects randomly assigned to the thrombectomy arm, except those with rapidly improving neurologic symptoms  or no angiographic evidence of occlusion, will be treated with endovascular thrombectomy, and will have the procedural imaging (pre-, intra-, post-procedure) for site evaluation of TICI flow at the start and end of the procedure. In the thrombectomy arm, the start of the procedure is the time the femoral artery is accessed (groin puncture), and it must occur  no  later  than  90  minutes  from  MRA/CTA  confirmation  of  the  occlusion.  After  femoral access is achieved, subjects will be administered IV heparin per institutional protocol, but it is recommended not exceed 2000 unit bolus and maximum 500 units per hour.  A microcatheter introduced over an appropriately sized guidewire can then be manipulated across the occlusive thrombus  under  high  magnification  roadmap  fluoroscopic  control.    After  removal  of  the microwire,  angiographic  runs  should  be  performed  per  standard  procedure  to  determine  the length  of  the  target  occlusion.    Site-assessed  TICI  scores  and  procedural  adverse  events  (if any) will be recorded on source documents for study.

texts.orig: The following sections provide a general description of the statistical  plan  for  the  analysis  of study data. A separate Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) document that provides greater detail of data derivations and analyses to be performed will be completed within one year of first subject enrollment and prior to the first interim analysis, which is planned when one third of the patients have completed the 3-months follow-up.  The SAP will reflect the protocol and any amendments implemented at the time the SAP is finalized.  Amendments to the SAP will be possible any time before the database is locked. Any deviations from the final SAP will be noted in the clinical study report.

texts.orig: Subjects  will  be  randomized  in  a  1:1  ratio  to  receive  best  medical  treatment  or  best  medical treatment  plus  thrombectomy.  Block  randomization  will  be  used,  stratified  by  stroke  severity (NIHSS 8-18 and >18), and time from symptom onset until randomization (< 6h and 6-11h of wake up stroke). Block lengths may vary, and details of the procedure are withheld from study personnel to retain allocation concealment as much as possible in this type of design.

texts.orig: The  following  have  been  defined  for  analysis:  an  Intent-to-Treat  (ITT)  analysis  set,  a  Safety analysis set, and a Per Protocol (PP) analysis set.  The primary endpoint shift analysis and all secondary endpoint efficacy analyses will be carried out in the ITT analysis set. Missing data will be imputed for the primary analysis. Supportive analyses of these endpoints will be carried out on the PP analysis set.  Interim analyses for early stopping are based on available data in the Intent-to-Treat analysis set.

texts.orig: In  general, summaries will be presented by treatment group pooled across occlusion location and investigators/sites, and by occlusion location within treatment group in the relevant analysis populations.  Descriptive statistics for dichotomous/categorical variables will include number and percent  of  subjects  in  each  category  (including  missing),  by  treatment  group.    Descriptive statistics  for  continuous  variables  will  include  number  of  non-missing  and  missing  subjects, minimum,  lower  quartile,  median,  upper  quartile,  maximum,  mean,  and  standard  deviation, stratified by treatment group.  Regarding comparisons between treatment groups, Chi-squared test  (Fisher's  exact  test  where  appropriate)  will  be  utilized  for  the  comparison  of  categorical variables and the t-test (or the Mann-Whitney U test when appropriate) will be utilized for the comparison  of  continuous  variables.    Data  for  the  primary  endpoint  will  be  presented  by treatment group (pooled over all sites) and by treatment group within study site . texts.orig: After  one  third  and  two  thirds  of  patients  have  completed  the  study,  respectively,  interim analyses take place to stop the trial for early success if a one-sided test suggests a treatment effect or for futility if the same test suggests that a rejection of the null hypothesis at the final analysis would be highly unlikely. The interim analysis pattern to be used will employ a power cumulative error spending function (Jennison, C. and Turnbull, B. W. (2000) Group Sequential Methods with Applications to Clinical Trials,  New  York:  Chapman & Hall), with a parameter ρ=3  (i.e.  similar  to  the  O'Brien  and  Fleming  sequential  plan)  for  alpha-spending  function (efficacy), and a parameter equal to 8 for the beta-spending function (futility).  The corresponding stopping boundaries (Z-values) at the 2 interim analyses and the final analysis are equal to 3.11, 2.46 and 2.01 for the alpha spending function (efficacy), and -2.38, -0.11 and  2.01  for  the  beta-pending  function  (futility). texts.label: text
texts.orig: An Adverse Event (AE) is any untoward medical occurrence in a study subject, user or other person,  and  which  does  not  necessarily  have  a  causal  relationship  with  the  product  or treatment;  any  unfavorable  and  unintended  sign,  symptom,  injury,  or  disease  temporally associated  with  the  treatment.  A  preexisting  condition  should  not  be  reported  as  an  adverse event unless the condition worsens or episodes increase in frequency during the adverse event reporting period.

texts.orig: In  order to provide for safe use of devices for thrombectomy the primary concern in operator selection  for  this  study  is  adequate  experience,  commitment  to  safety,  and  consistency  in adherence  to  the  clinical  protocol.  Therefore,  the  interventional  investigators  selected  to participate  will  be  neurointerventionalists  who,  by  virtue  of  their  experience  and  training,  are accomplished  in  cerebral  flow  restoration  techniques  using  neurothrombectomy  devices  in intracranial  arteries.  Each  qualified  center  must  conduct  at  least  50  neurothrombectomy procedures  each  year.  Each  interventional  investigator  will  be  experienced,  and  will  have participated  in  at  least  50  neurothrombectomy  procedures  overall.  For  every  thrombectomy device used in the study, at least 15 previous procedures must have been performed by the interventionalist.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.2.1 The normal case and the problem of patients unable to give informed consent
texts.text: 9.2.1 The normal case and the problem of patients unable to give informed consent

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Informed consent has to be obtained prior to enrolment of patients in TENSION. In the normal case written consent will be given by the patient after detailed information about the clinical trial by the investigator. However, given the sample to be studied (i.e. acute stroke patients showing neurological  deficits  that  may  comprise  aphasia  or  disturbance  of  consciousness)  we  expect that a certain proportion of patients (estimated 40-60%) will be unable to give informed consent. Excluding this group of patients from the clinical trial would entail severe scientific and clinical drawbacks.  Results  would  be  biased  by  systematically  excluding  more  severe  strokes  and patients with aphasia, i.e. mostly left hemispheric strokes. As a consequence, the generalizability  of  the  study  results  would  be  limited.  Strictly  speaking,  in  case  of  a  positive result this could not be transferred to the patients excluded from the trial (e.g. aphasic patients). This large group would still be excluded from this effective treatment.

texts.orig: 9.2.2 Enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent - general considerations
texts.text: 9.2.2 Enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent - general considerations

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A possible solution would allow the enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent based on  their  alleged  will  following  pre-specified  criteria.  These  criteria  would  have  to  consider  a potential  individual  benefit  as  well  as  any  possible  risk  of  participation  in  the  clinical  trial.  In general the protection of the patient and his autonomy has to be weighed against the potential individual benefit as well as the scientific interest. Following European and national regulations the  enrolment  of  patient  (temporarily)  unable  to  give  informed  consent  into  clinical  trials  is possible  in  an  emergency  situation  if  a  legal  guardian  is  not  available  and  -  after  careful consideration of possible risks and potential individual benefit - a participation in the clinical trial would comply with the patient's presumptive will. Moreover, standard treatment following best medical practice must not be withheld to the patient by enrolment in the clinical trial.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For patients eligible for enrolment in TENSION best medical practice in these patients usually comprises i.e. thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours, if indicated) and hospitalization and monitoring in a  specialized  stroke  unit.  Standard  treatment  consists  of  supervision  and  modification  of physiological parameters (such as blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose) and early secondary prevention (e.g. Aspirin).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.2.3 Potential individual benefit and risk of participation in TENSION
texts.text: 9.2.3 Potential individual benefit and risk of participation in TENSION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients enrolled in TENSION will be randomized based on a 1:1 ration to treatment with best medical  care  alone  or  best  medical  care  plus  thrombectomy.  All  patients  receive  standard treatment  according  to  European  and  national  guidelines  (see  above)  independent  from  the result  of  randomization.  In  addition  to  standard  treatment,  there  is  a  50%  chance  to  receive treatment with thrombectomy. This treatment brings a potential benefit for the patient (as the hypothesis to be tested in TENSION which was based on promising results from randomized trials  in  patients  with  good  prognostic  factors  treated  with  thrombectomy  will  have  a  good outcome 90 days after stroke). Two recent randomized clinical trials showed that endovascular therapy compared to standard medical therapy alone in an extended time window up to 16 or 24 hours after patient last know well was associated with a higher percentage of patients who were functionally independent and in a favorable mRS shift (Nogueira et al. 2018, Albers et al. 2018). So there is a potential individual benefit foreseeable by participating in TENSION. However, so far no randomized control trial showed a clinical benefit in patients with large infarcts and in an extended time window undergoing thrombectomy compared to best medical care.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The potential risk of participation in the clinical trial can be estimated based on the risk of the thrombectomy  procedure.  All  recent  trials  (Synthesis,  IMS  3,  MR  Rescue,  MR  CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND -IA, SWIFT Prime) comparing thrombectomy to standard care all safety endpoints  did  not  differ  between  treatment  groups.  Therefore,  no  major  additional  risk  is associated with the inclusion in the thrombectomy arm in TENSION.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If  the  patient  is  unable  to  give  informed  consent  and  no  legal  guardian  has  been appointed, the patient may be enrolled by consensus between the investigator and an independent physician.  If possible, patient's next of kin should be contacted to appraise the  patient's  presumed  will;  the  decision  has  to  be  documented  using  a  special  form. Immediately parallel an application for appointing a legal guardian will be started later, patient or legal guardian will be informed by the investigator and may or may not provide written  consent.  This  mode  of  consent  will  be  applied  to  minimize  inclusion  bias. Otherwise, especially older and more severely affected patients would be excluded from the  trial  (Flaherty  et  al.  2008,  Mendyk  et  al.  2015,  Hotter  et  al.  2017,  Thomalla  et  al. 2018).  TENSION  aims  to  include  patients  with  moderately  sever  to  severe  stroke.  A large majority of these patients will have diminished decision-making capacity due to a reduced  level  of  consciousness,  aphasia  or  other  cognitive  disorders.  Only  very  few patients will be accompanied by a legal guardian at the time of hospital admission. Since acute  ischemic  stroke  is  a  medical  emergency  the  treatment  decision  cannot  be postponed  to  await  the  appointment  of  a  legal  guardian.  Excluding  these  specific subgroups of stroke patients would result in a study population that is not representative of  acute  stroke  patients  in  general.  It  would  also  lead  to  a  systematic  exclusion  of patients with certain types of neurological deficit (i.e. aphasia). Therefore, exclusion of this  patient  subgroup  would  lead  to  a  loss  of  generalizability  and  slower  recruitment rates.

texts.text: Stroke: Signs  of  focal  cerebral  or  retinal  ischemia  persisting  for  24  hours  or  more.    A  stroke  is considered disabling if the modified Rankin score is 3 or greater

texts.text: Symptomatic Intracranial Hemorrhage (SITS-MOST): SICH at 30 (-/+ 6) hours (CT or MRI) as defined in SITS-MOST ('local or remote parenchymal hematoma type 2 on the imaging scan obtained 22 to 36 hours after treatment, plus neurologic deterioration, as indicated by a score on the NIHSS ≥ 4 points than the baseline value or the lowest value between baseline and 24 hours, or haemorrhage leading to death') (Wahlgren et al., 2007)

texts.label: text

texts.text: Symptomatic Intracranial Hemorrhage (ECASS II): SICH at 30 (-/+ 6) hours (CT or MRI) as defined in ECASS II ('any hemorrhage with neurologic deterioration, as indicated by an NIHSS score ≥ 4 points than the value at baseline or the lowest value in the first 7 days, or any hemorrhage leading to death') (Hacke et al., 1998)

texts.orig: TICI 0: No perfusion - No antegrade flow beyond the point of occlusion.
texts.text: TICI 0: No perfusion - No antegrade flow beyond the point of occlusion.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TICI 1: Penetration  with  minimal perfusion - The contrast material passes beyond the area of obstruction but fails to opacify the entire cerebral bed distal to the obstruction for the duration of the angiographic run.
texts.text: TICI 1: Penetration  with  minimal perfusion - The contrast material passes beyond the area of obstruction but fails to opacify the entire cerebral bed distal to the obstruction for the duration of the angiographic run.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TICI 2: Partial perfusion - The contrast material passes beyond the obstruction and opacifies the arterial bed distal to the obstruction.  However, the rate of entry of contrast into the vessel distal to the obstruction and/or its rate of clearance from the distal bed are perceptibly slower than its entry  into  and/or  clearance  from  comparable  areas  not  perfused  by  the  previously  occluded vessel (e.g., the opposite cerebral artery or the arterial bed proximal to the obstruction).
texts.text: TICI 2: Partial perfusion - The contrast material passes beyond the obstruction and opacifies the arterial bed distal to the obstruction.  However, the rate of entry of contrast into the vessel distal to the obstruction and/or its rate of clearance from the distal bed are perceptibly slower than its entry  into  and/or  clearance  from  comparable  areas  not  perfused  by  the  previously  occluded vessel (e.g., the opposite cerebral artery or the arterial bed proximal to the obstruction).

texts.label: text

texts.text: TICI 2a: Only partial filling - <50% of the entire vascular territory is opacified .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The prognosis following an acute ischemic stroke varies, depending on the stroke severity and the individual's premorbid condition, age, and post stroke complications (Adams 1999). In the United States, 20% of individuals die within the first year after a first-time stroke.  The Framingham Heart Study showed that among stroke survivors, 31% needed help caring for themselves, 20% needed  help  when  walking,  and  71%  had  impaired  vocational  capacity  when  examined  an average 7 years following the stroke.

texts.orig: For  years,  intravenous  thrombolysis  with  recombinant  tissue  Plasminogen  Activator  (rtPA, Alteplase)  represented  the  only  effective  and  approved  specific  treatment  for  acute  ischemic stroke  and  is  recommended  by  international,  European  and  national  guidelines  (ESO,  2008). Following the first positive clinical trial of thrombolysis in ischemic stroke, treatment with Alteplase was  restricted  to  treatment  initiation  ≤3  hours  of  symptom  onset  but  based  on  the  results  of ECASS III (Hacke et al., 2008) international guidelines now recommend intravenous thrombolysis up  to  4.5  hours  of  symptom  onset  (Del  Zoppo  et  al.,  2009).  Consequently,  the  European Medicines Agency has approved intravenous thrombolysis with Alteplase for acute stroke up to 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

texts.orig: In large vessel occlusions, however, recanalization after i.v. thrombolysis is infrequent and in a thrombus  length  of  more  than  8  mm  almost  absent  (Riedel  et  al.,  2011).  Since  timely recanalization is crucial for a good outcome in stroke alternative therapy is warranted in patients with large vessel occlusion. Moreover, a substantial number of patients cannot receive i.v. tPA for contraindications  (e.g.  anticoagulation,  recent  surgery,  time  after  symptom  onset  beyond  4.5 hours). In these patient groups endovascular mechanical clot removal has been advocated. The first generation devices (Merci, Penumbra) achieved recanalization in up to 50%; however, clinical outcome was not substantially  improved  compared  to  historical  controls  (Smith  et  al.,  Stroke 2005). Safety of endovascular treatment with mechanical or pharmacological approaches was also comparable in patients under oral anticoagulants (de Marchis et al., 2011). Stent-like devices for thrombectomy also referred to as stent-retrievers have substantially improved recanalization rates and outcome compared to first generation devices (Nogueira et al., 2012, Saver et al., 2012). Recently, 5 RCTs mostly using thrombectomy by stent retrievers in the endovascular treatment of acute stroke compared to best medical care demonstrated overwhelming clinical benefit without increased  adverse  events  (Berkhemer  et  al.,  2015,  Goyal  et  al.,  2015,  Saver  et  al.,  2015, Campbell  et  al.,  2015,  Jovin  et  al,  2015). texts.label: text
texts.orig: CLEAN only small numbers of patients with low ASPECTS values were included. In 28 patients with ASPECTS 0-4 no treatment effect was evident with an OR of 1.1 (95% CI 0.1-8.4) for benefit in the thrombectomy group, while in 92 patients with ASPECTS 5-7 with an OR of 2.0 (0.9-4.4) a clear trend for a treatment benefit was observed similar to the effect in the group of patients with ASPECTS >7 (Berkhemer et al., 2015). Thus, based on the data from these trials, insufficient evidence is available to judge whether mechanical thrombectomy is also safe and effective in patients with an extended time window or advanced signs of early ischemia, or a combination of both. This was also acknowledged by experts from the European Stroke Organisation (ESO), the European  Society  for  Minimally  Invasive  Neurological  Therapy  (ESMINT),  and  the  European Society of Neuroradiology (ESNR) a consensus statement on thrombectomy (Wahlgren et al, 2016).  In  this  statement  the  experts  clearly  recommend  further  randomized  clinical  trials addressing open issues such as 'treatment in a late und unknown time windows, treating patients with imaging findings not sufficiently covered in recent trials…'. TENSION aims to close this gap and provide evidence for thrombectomy in in both late time window and patients with more extend early ischemic signs before treatment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This is an investigator-initiated, prospective, European, two-arm, randomized, controlled, open label, blinded endpoint post-market study to compare  the  safety and  effectiveness of endovascular thrombectomy compared to best medical treatment alone in acute ischemic stroke (AIS) patients with extended stroke lesions up to 12 hours of symptom onset or last seen well. Patients who meet the inclusion criteria will be randomized to one of the following two treatment arms: best medical care alone or best medical care plus endovascular treatment with devices for endovascular thrombectomy (referred to as thrombectomy). Endpoints in this prospective open label study will be assessed blinded to the treatment assignment of the patient (PROBE design). This study will be conducted in approximately 40 sites in eight to ten European countries.  This is an adaptive design study, in which there are prospectively stated interim analyses with specified stopping rules, which allow for the possibility of the study to terminate early based on either a determination of study success or of the futility to continue further enrollment.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All subjects randomly assigned to the thrombectomy arm, except those with rapidly improving neurologic symptoms or no angiographic evidence of occlusion, will be treated with endovascular thrombectomy,  and  will  have  the  procedural  imaging  (pre-,  intra-,  post-procedure)  for  site evaluation of TICI flow at the start and end of the procedure. In the thrombectomy arm, the start of the procedure is the time the femoral artery is accessed (groin puncture), and it must occur no later  than  90  minutes  from  MRA/CTA  confirmation  of  the  occlusion.  After  femoral  access  is achieved, subjects will be administered IV heparin per institutional protocol, but it is recommended not exceed 2000 unit bolus and maximum 500 units per hour.  A microcatheter introduced over an appropriately sized guidewire can then be manipulated across the occlusive thrombus under high magnification roadmap fluoroscopic control.  After removal of the microwire, angiographic runs should be performed per standard procedure to determine the length of the target occlusion. Site-assessed TICI scores and procedural adverse events (if any) will be recorded on source documents for study.

texts.orig: The primary effectiveness endpoint analysis (referred to as a 'mRS shift' analysis) is carried out as  a  parameter  test  in  the  ordinal  logistic  regression  model  with  the  mRS  ordinal  scale  as response variable and treatment group, stroke severity (NIHSS 8-18 and NIHSS >18), time from symptom onset until randomization (0-6 hours and 6-11hours) as explanatory variables.  For this mRS shift analysis, ordinal mRS outcomes in categories 5 and 6 are pooled into one category 5. The null and alternative hypotheses for this primary endpoint are H0: β=0 and HA: β≠0, where β is the parameter for the treatment effect in the logistic model. This model is based on the assumption of proportional odds, with constant underlying treatment effect (odds ratio) at any level of the MRS scale. The treatment effect will be tested using the likelihood ratio test of the treatment parameter. In a secondary analysis, the primary analysis will be repeated for the per protocol population.

The interim analysis pattern to be used will employ a power cumulative error spending function (Jennison, C. and Turnbull, B. W. (2000) Group Sequential Methods with Applications to Clinical Trials, New York: Chapman & Hall), with a parameter ρ=3 (i.e. similar to the O'Brien and Fleming sequential plan) for alpha-spending function (efficacy), and a parameter equal to 8 for the beta-spending function (futility). texts.orig: An Adverse Event (AE) is any untoward medical occurrence in a study subject, user or other person, and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the product or treatment; any unfavorable and unintended sign, symptom, injury, or disease temporally associated with the treatment. texts.orig: In  order to  provide for  safe  use  of  devices for  thrombectomy the primary concern in operator selection  for  this  study  is  adequate  experience,  commitment  to  safety,  and  consistency  in adherence  to  the  clinical  protocol.  Therefore,  the  interventional  investigators  selected  to participate  will  be  neurointerventionalists  who,  by  virtue  of  their  experience  and  training,  are accomplished  in  cerebral  flow  restoration  techniques  using  neurothrombectomy  devices  in intracranial  arteries.  Each  qualified  center  must  conduct  at  least  50  neurothrombectomy procedures  each  year.  Each  interventional  investigator  will  be  experienced,  and  will  have participated  in  at  least  50  neurothrombectomy  procedures  overall.  For  every  thrombectomy device used in the study, at least 15 previous procedures must have been performed by the interventionalist.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.2.1 The normal case and the problem of patients unable to give informed consent
texts.text: 9.2.1 The normal case and the problem of patients unable to give informed consent

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Informed consent has to be obtained prior to enrolment of patients in TENSION. In the normal case written consent will be given by the patient after detailed information about the clinical trial by the investigator. However, given the sample to be studied (i.e. acute stroke patients showing neurological deficits that may comprise aphasia or disturbance of consciousness) we expect that a  certain  proportion  of  patients  (estimated  40-60%)  will  be  unable  to  give  informed  consent. Excluding this group of patients from the clinical trial would entail severe scientific and clinical drawbacks.  Results  would  be  biased  by  systematically  excluding  more  severe  strokes  and patients with aphasia, i.e. mostly left hemispheric strokes. As a consequence, the generalizability of the study results would be limited. Strictly speaking, in case of a positive result this could not be transferred to the patients excluded from the trial (e.g. aphasic patients). This large group would still be excluded from this effective treatment.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.2.2 Enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent -general considerations
texts.text: 9.2.2 Enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent -general considerations

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A possible solution would allow the enrolment of patients unable to give informed consent based on  their  alleged  will  following  pre-specified  criteria.  These  criteria  would  have  to  consider  a potential individual benefit as well as any possible risk of participation in the clinical trial. In general the protection of the patient and his autonomy has to be weighed against the potential individual benefit  as  well  as  the  scientific  interest.  Following  European  and  national  regulations  the enrolment of patient (temporarily) unable to give informed consent into clinical trials is possible in an emergency situation if a legal guardian is not available and - after careful consideration of possible risks and potential individual benefit - a participation in the clinical trial would comply with the patient's presumptive will. Moreover, standard treatment following best medical practice must not be withheld to the patient by enrolment in the clinical trial.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For patients eligible for enrolment in TENSION best medical practice in these patients usually comprises i.e. thrombolysis (within 4.5 hours, if indicated) and hospitalization and monitoring in a specialized stroke unit. Standard  treatment  consists of supervision and  modification of physiological parameters (such as blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose) and early secondary prevention (e.g. Aspirin).

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 9.2.3 Potential individual benefit and risk of participation in TENSION
texts.text: 9.2.3 Potential individual benefit and risk of participation in TENSION

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients enrolled in TENSION will be randomized based on a 1:1 ration to treatment with best medical  care  alone  or  best  medical  care  plus  thrombectomy.  All  patients  receive  standard treatment according to European and national guidelines (see above) independent from the result of randomization. In addition to standard treatment, there is a 50% chance to receive treatment with thrombectomy. This treatment brings a potential benefit for the patient (as the hypothesis to be tested in TENSION which was based on promising results from randomized trials in patients with good prognostic factors treated with thrombectomy will have a good outcome 90 days after stroke). Two recent randomized clinical trials showed that endovascular therapy compared to standard medical therapy alone in an extended time window up to 16 or 24 hours after patient last  know  well  was  associated  with  a  higher  percentage  of  patients  who  were  functionally independent and in a favorable mRS shift (Nogueira et al. 2018, Albers et al. 2018). So there is a potential  individual  benefit  foreseeable  by  participating  in  TENSION.  However,  so  far  no randomized control trial showed a clinical benefit in patients with large infarcts and in an extended time window undergoing thrombectomy compared to best medical care.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The potential risk of participation in the clinical trial can be estimated based on the risk of the thrombectomy procedure. All recent trials (Synthesis, IMS 3, MR Rescue, MR CLEAN, ESCAPE, EXTEND -IA, SWIFT Prime) comparing thrombectomy to standard care all safety endpoints did not differ between treatment groups. Therefore, no major additional risk is associated with the inclusion in the thrombectomy arm in TENSION.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the patient is unable to give informed consent and no legal guardian has been appointed, the patient may be enrolled by consensus between the investigator and an independent physician.  If possible, patient's next of kin should be contacted to appraise the patient's presumed  will;  the  decision  has  to  be  documented  using  a  special  form.  Immediately parallel an application for appointing a legal guardian will be started later, patient or legal guardian will be informed by the investigator and may or may not provide written consent. This mode of consent will be applied to minimize inclusion bias. Otherwise, especially older and more severely affected patients would be excluded from the trial (Flaherty et al. 2008, Mendyk et al. 2015, Hotter et al. 2017, Thomalla et al. 2018). TENSION aims to include patients with moderately sever to severe stroke. A large majority of these patients will have diminished decision-making capacity due to a reduced level of consciousness, aphasia or other cognitive disorders. Only very few patients will be accompanied by a legal guardian at the time of hospital admission. Since acute ischemic stroke is a medical emergency the treatment decision cannot be postponed to await the appointment of a legal guardian. Excluding these specific subgroups of stroke patients would result in a study population that  is  not  representative  of  acute  stroke  patients  in  general.  It  would  also  lead  to  a systematic exclusion of patients with certain types of neurological  deficit (i.e. aphasia). Therefore, exclusion of this patient subgroup would lead to a loss of generalizability and slower recruitment rates.

texts.text: TICI 1: Penetration  with  minimal perfusion  - The contrast material passes beyond the area of obstruction but fails to opacify the entire cerebral bed distal to the obstruction for the duration of the angiographic run.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TICI 2: Partial perfusion - The contrast material passes beyond the obstruction and opacifies the arterial bed distal to the obstruction.  However, the rate of entry of contrast into the vessel distal to the obstruction and/or its rate of clearance from the distal bed are perceptibly slower than its entry into and/or clearance from comparable areas not perfused by the previously occluded vessel (e.g., the opposite cerebral artery or the arterial bed proximal to the obstruction).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The TENSION trial is aimed to recruit 660 patients from about 40 centres in 8 to 10 european countries, hence an average of 16 patients per centre. However, it is likely that many centres will recruit far fewer patients, while a small number of big centres will recruit much more. Such a situation is an argument for not adjusting the primary analysis on centres. As ICH9 guideline quotes:
texts.text: The TENSION trial is aimed to recruit 660 patients from about 40 centres in 8 to 10 european countries, hence an average of 16 patients per centre. However, it is likely that many centres will recruit far fewer patients, while a small number of big centres will recruit much more. Such a situation is an argument for not adjusting the primary analysis on centres. As ICH9 guideline quotes:

texts.label: text

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TENSION is an investigator-initiated, prospective, open label, blinded endpoint (PROBE), multinational, European, two-arm, randomized, controlled, post-market clinical trial. Patients will be randomized 1:1 to either best medical care + endovascular thrombectomy or best medical care alone. It is planned to recruit 665 patients in approximately 40 sites in eight to ten European countries, to be followed-up for 12 months.

texts.orig: The TENSION trial is aimed to recruit 660 patients from about 40 centres in 8 to 10 european countries, hence an average of 16 patients per centre. Such a situation is an argument for not adjusting the primary analysis on centres. As ICH9 guideline quotes:

texts.text: The primary effectiveness endpoint for a subject is the blinded evaluation of the ordinal mRS outcome at 90 (+/-14) days post-stroke ( MRS.QSORRES, SVSEQ=7).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The primary effectiveness endpoint analysis (referred to as a 'mRS shift' analysis) is carried out as a parameter test in a proportional-odds logistic regression model with the mRS ordinal scale as response variable and treatment group, stroke severity (NIHSS 8-18 and NIHSS >18) ( IC.STRAT1) , time from symptom onset until randomization (0-6 hours and 611hours)( IC.STRAT2 ) as explanatory variables.  For this mRS shift analysis, ordinal mRS outcomes in categories 0 and 1 are pooled into one category. If the model does not converge, categories 0, 1 and 2 are pooled into one category.  The null and alternative hypotheses for this primary endpoint are H0: β=0 and HA: β≠0, where β is the parameter for the treatment effect in the logistic model. This model is based on the assumption of proportional odds, with constant underlying treatment effect (odds ratio) at any level of the MRS scale (Agresti, A. (2002), Categorical Data Analysis, Second Edition, New York: John Wiley & Sons). If the assumption of proportional odds is not fulfilled for any variable of the model (treatment group or stratification variables), different sets of coefficients will be included in the model to describe the relationship between each pair of outcome groups for the variables for which the hypothesis is not fulfilled.  The treatment effect will be tested using the likelihood ratio test of the treatment parameter. The Wald confidence interval of the treatment effect will be provided, with coverage probability in accordance with the nominal alpha level of the final analysis .
